A condolence is an expression of sympathy and sorrow that you offer to someone who has just experienced a loss — most commonly the death of a loved one. When you express a condolence, you are essentially saying: "I know you are in pain, I feel for you, and I share in your grief."

It is not advice. It is not a solution. It is simply an act of emotional acknowledgment — letting a grieving person know that their pain matters to others and that they are not alone in it.

Condolences are offered specifically in response to loss and grief. The most common situation is the death of someone close — a parent, spouse, child, friend, or colleague. However, the word can also be used for other serious losses, such as a devastating illness, a miscarriage, or even the death of a beloved pet, though this is less common.

You would not use condolences for everyday disappointments like failing a test or losing a job (though those are sad events). The word carries a weight of gravity — it is reserved for deep, profound loss.
Singular vs. plural — an important detail

In everyday English, "condolences" (the plural form) is far more common than the singular "condolence." You will almost always see it in the plural:

  • "Please accept my condolences."
  • "I offered my condolences to the family."

When the singular is used, it usually appears with the word "a" or in formal writing:

  • "He expressed a condolence that felt sincere."

Think of it this way: just as people say "my thanks" rather than "my thank," people say "my condolences" as a set phrase. The plural form has become the standard.
How it is used in sentences

Here are natural examples of the word in real-life contexts:

  • "When her father passed away, her colleagues sent flowers and their condolences."
  • "I called him to offer my condolences after hearing about his loss."
  • "Please convey my deepest condolences to the grieving family."
  • "The president expressed his condolences to the victims' families."
  • "She received hundreds of condolence messages from around the world." (Here, "condolence" is used as an adjective modifying "messages.")
  • "His condolences felt hollow — just empty words without real feeling."

Notice how the word is often paired with verbs like offer, express, send, extend, or convey.
Common phrases built around this word

These are set phrases you will encounter very frequently in real life:

  • "My condolences" — the most common and simple way to express sympathy directly to someone grieving.
  • "My deepest condolences" — a more heartfelt, emphatic version; "deepest" intensifies the sincerity.
  • "My sincere condolences" — stresses that the sympathy is genuine.
  • "Please accept my condolences" — a slightly more formal phrasing, often used in written messages.
  • "A condolence card / condolence message / condolence letter" — a card, message, or letter specifically written to someone who is grieving.
  • "A condolence visit" — when you visit someone in person to offer comfort after a loss.

It helps to understand what the word does not mean:

  • It is not a compliment — it does not celebrate anything.
  • It is not advice — saying "you should be strong" is not a condolence; it is advice.
  • It is not the same as sympathy alone — sympathy means you feel sorry for someone; a condolence is specifically a formal or verbal expression of that sympathy in the context of loss. You feel sympathy silently in your heart; you express a condolence outward.
  • It is not casual — condolences carry a formal, serious tone. You would not say "condolences on missing the bus" as a joke unless you were being deliberately theatrical.

A condolence is a gentle, human gesture. It doesn't pretend to fix anything or take the pain away. It simply says: "I see what you're going through. I care."

When someone has lost a person they loved, there are no words that truly heal the wound. A condolence acknowledges this truth — it doesn't try to make everything okay; it just stands beside the grieving person in their sorrow. This is why condolences are so important: they are one of the few moments in language where we reach out not to inform or persuade, but simply to be present with another human being in their darkest moment.

What it isAn expression of sympathy offered to someone who has suffered a loss
Used forDeath, grief, profound loss
Common formAlmost always used in the plural — condolences
ToneFormal, sincere, serious
Key verbs with itOffer, express, send, extend, convey
It is NOTAdvice, a casual remark, or empty without genuine feeling behind it

Condolence is one of the most human words in the English language — it exists because we need a way to reach out to those who are hurting and say, without pretense: "Your grief is real, and you are not alone."
